newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Klima reopens tender for CA sale.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Klima reopens tender for CA sale.

text.p: The sale of Austria's second biggest bank, Creditanstalt Bankverein, took a new twist on Friday when Finance Minister Viktor Klima reopened the tender to give bidders more time to improve their offers.
The Finance Ministry said in a statement that a new deadline had been set for January 10.
"In order to secure the best proceeds (for the sale), the Finance Ministry decided to allow one last chance for the offers to be improved," the statement said.
The decision appeared to head off deepening conflict between the ruling Social Democrats and their junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, over the sale.

Market leader Bank Austria, effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna, is up against rival offers from a consortium led by Austro-Italian insurer EA Generali favoured by the conservatives, and Austrian entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek, an outsider.
"It sounds like they want the consortium to pay a bit more which it probably will do," said Austria analyst Victoria Maxwell at James Capel in London.
"Maybe there are political reasons why they don't want to give it to Bank Austria, that's why they're holding off to see if EA-Generali will make a more attractive offer," she added.
The finance ministry also made public for the first time the offers put in by two of the three bidders.

It said Bank Austria had made an offer of 836 schillings per share for the whole of the government's 70 percent of ordinary shares in the flagship bank, amounting to a total of 16.7 billion schillings ($1.53 billion).
The state's holding is worth 14.5 billion schillings at market prices.

The consortium had offered 730 schillings per share for 14.7 million shares and 580 schillings for the remaining 5.2 million shares, which it planned to float on the stock market, the finance ministry said.
The bid by unfancied dark horse Wlaschek was not disclosed but has been estimated at around 15 billion schillings.

The consortium declined to make any immediate comment on whether it would raise its bid. "We will analyse the information the finance minister gave us," EA Generali spokesman Josef Hlinka told Reuters.
Bank Austria was not immediately available for comment.
The announcement came after off-and-on talks on Friday between Klima, a senior Social Democrat, and Economics Minister Johannes Farnleitner of the conservative People's Party.

The ill-fated privatisation of conservative stronghold Creditanstalt, which has been dragging on for six years, took on a political hue when "socialist" Bank Austria entered the fray shortly before the December 16 deadline for bids, creating fresh tension in the coalition.

"Finance Minister Klima made the decision on his own but it does not close the way for a common solution for an efficient and economically sensible privatisation of Creditanstalt," Farnleitner said in a statement after Friday's announcement.
Klima had previously insisted he would wind up the sale by year-end but strains within the coalition appeared to have prompted the finance minister to reopen the bidding.
Conservative politicians had threatened to call an emergency session of parliament and a no-confidence vote if Klima accepted the Bank Austria bid.

Austrian daily Der Standard reported last week that the consortium, which includes savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian), Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana, hoped to raise an extra three billion schillings. ($1=10.93 Schilling)
